chapters.title: You don't have to quit today
chapters.text:
[warmly] Hi. I'm really glad you're here. [pause]

For the next seven days, I'll be with you for a few minutes in the morning and a few minutes in the evening. And I want to start with the thing that surprises most people. [pause] You don't have to quit today. You don't have to quit tomorrow, either.

For the whole of this week, you keep {s: smoking | v: vaping | p: using pouches} exactly as you do now. Same amount, same times, same places. No cutting down. No counting the hours with your jaw clenched.

That might sound odd, coming from a program that's meant to help you stop. So here's why. [pause] It's very hard to look clearly at something while you're fighting it. When you try to stop before you understand what's going on, every {s: cigarette | v: puff | p: pouch} you can't have starts to look more precious, not less. So this week, we look first. We take the habit apart, piece by piece, while it's still right there in your hand. Then, on your Quit Day, you stop. Not because you've run out of reasons to keep going, but because you've seen what it really was.

You might feel some relief hearing that. You might feel a bit of doubt, too. Both are fine. You can be unsure and still be here. And if part of you is thinking, "I'll believe it when I see it," good. That's exactly the attitude this week needs.

chapters.title: This was never about willpower
chapters.text:
Maybe you've tried before. Maybe more than once. If it didn't last, I want to say this clearly. [pause] That doesn't mean you're weak.

Nicotine is highly addictive. It works fast, it wears off fast, and it teaches your brain to want it back, over and over, many times a day. That's not a flaw in you. It's how the drug works.

And trying to quit on willpower alone is a hard way to go about it. A review of studies on people who tried to quit without any help found that only about three to five in every hundred of those attempts lasted six months to a year. [pause] Hear that the right way. It doesn't mean quitting is rare. Millions of people have quit. It means that gritting your teeth, on your own, against something you don't fully understand, is a poor tool for the job.

So we're going to use better tools. Understanding first. Then skills for the hard moments. Then setting up your space and your support. People who stay quit aren't made of stronger stuff. They tend to see it differently, and they're better prepared. That's what this week is for.

chapters.title: The gap
chapters.text:
[calmly] Let me show you the first piece. I call it the gap.

Nicotine leaves your body fairly quickly. In about two hours, roughly half of it is gone. And as the level drops, a feeling arrives. [pause] It's a little restless. A little empty. Slightly on edge, as if something isn't quite finished. It's hard to settle, hard to focus.

It's mild. So mild that it's easy to go years without putting a name to it. It just feels like, "I could do with one." And because it comes back every hour or two, all day long, it starts to feel like your normal. Like that's just how you are.

Then you {s: light up | v: take a hit | p: put one in}, and within {s: seconds | v: seconds | p: a few minutes}, that feeling settles. And the settling feels good. It feels like pleasure, or calm, or focus. [pause] That relief is real. I'm not going to tell you you're imagining it.

But here's the part I'd like you to sit with. What it relieves is the gap the last one opened.

Think of a faucet dripping in another room. After a while you stop hearing it, but part of you stays a little tense. When someone finally turns it off, the quiet feels wonderful. [pause] But a person in a house with no dripping faucet already has that quiet. All day long. They don't feel it as a treat, because nothing was missing.

People who don't use nicotine don't have the gap. They aren't holding back or going without. There's simply nothing pulling at them. [pause] And that's where you're heading. Not to a life with something missing. To a life without the gap.

chapters.title: Today: just watch
chapters.text:
So, today. There's one thing I'd like you to do, and it's small. [pause]

Keep using as normal. But a few times today, before you {s: light up | v: take a hit | p: put one in}, take one slow breath and ask yourself two questions. How much of this is the gap? And where do I feel it? Your chest, your throat, your hands, your head. [pause] There are no right answers. Some will feel mostly like the gap. Some won't. You're just collecting evidence. If you notice the gap, good. If you can't find it, that's useful too. Either way, you've looked, and looking is the whole job today.

You don't have to believe a word I've said yet. I'd much rather you find out for yourself.

In a moment, you'll set up three of these check-ins, and bring your reasons along with you. And this evening, there's a short track to look back on what you noticed.

[warmly] That's it for this morning. Keep using. Just watch.

deck.title: Why the first one feels so good
deck.intro: Four questions about that first one. Tap each card to turn it over.

cards.front: Why does the first one of the day hit so hard?
cards.answer: Because you wake up in the gap. A night without nicotine leaves the level low, so the first {s: cigarette | v: hit | p: pouch} has the most to close. That's why it feels like the best one.
cards.deeper: Nicotine wears off quickly: about half of it is gone in two hours or so. After seven or eight hours of sleep, very little is left. You don't feel the gap much while you're asleep, so you wake up in the middle of it, often without noticing. Then the first one of the day closes the widest gap you'll have all day, all at once. The relief is bigger, so it feels like the best one. It isn't adding more than the others. There's just more to fill. Tomorrow you'll look at the other half of the story: the morning routine that comes with it.

cards.front: How does someone who doesn't use nicotine wake up?
cards.answer: Without the gap. Their morning can still be tired, rushed or grumpy, but nothing is tugging at them, and there's no sense of something they need to sort out first.
cards.deeper: It's easy to assume that people who don't use are going without something every morning. They aren't. They never built the gap, so there's nothing to close. They have the same alarms, the same tired mornings, the same coffee. What they don't have is an extra layer of restlessness waiting to be fixed before the day can start. That's worth picturing, because it's where you're heading. Not a morning with something missing. A morning without the tug. From Day Xero on, you get to find out what that feels like.

cards.front: If it's just the gap, why does it feel like it helps?
cards.answer: Because relief is a real feeling. Going from on edge to settled feels good, it happens quickly, and it happens many times a day. Your brain files that as "this helps."
cards.deeper: Relief is one of the most convincing feelings there is. You feel a bit off, you use, you feel better, and the timing is so neat that the conclusion seems obvious. Now repeat that, say, a dozen times a day. That's more than four thousand times a year, each one a small lesson that says "this is what makes me feel right." Nobody would come away from that much practice believing anything else. So it isn't foolish to feel that it helps. The feeling is honest. It's the explanation underneath it that's worth checking: was it adding something, or ending something it started?

cards.front: Do I have to stop believing it helps, starting today?
cards.answer: No. You can hold both. It feels like it helps, and you're curious what it's actually helping with. Beliefs loosen with evidence, not force. This week is for gathering it.
cards.deeper: You can't argue yourself out of a feeling, and you don't need to. This week, thoughts like "I need one" or "this is the only thing that settles me" will keep showing up. Let them. You might even say to yourself, "I'm having the thought that I need one." That small step back turns a command into something you can look at. Meanwhile, you keep using as normal and you keep watching. Each check-in, each moment you notice the gap closing, is a piece of your own evidence. By Day Xero the aim is that you see it differently because you've seen it for yourself, not because anyone told you to.

deck.title: What you've been told
deck.intro: Five things people often believe about nicotine. Tap Myth or Fact. There's no score.

statements.text: I {s: smoke | v: vape | p: use pouches} because I enjoy it.
statements.verdict: The relief is real. Mostly, it's the gap closing.
statements.explanation: You're not imagining the good feeling, and moments like a break or a chat can be genuinely pleasant. But nicotine wears off quickly, and as it does it leaves a restless, slightly empty feeling. Using ends that feeling within {s: seconds | v: seconds | p: minutes}, and the ending feels like pleasure. People who don't use don't have that feeling to end. Your check-ins today are a way to test this for yourself.

statements.text: It's just a habit.
statements.verdict: It's a habit and a drug, working together.
statements.explanation: The habit part is real: the coffee, the car, the break at work. But nicotine is also a drug your brain adapts to, so when the level drops you feel a pull to top it up. The habit decides when; the drug makes you want it. That's why trying harder often isn't enough on its own, and why this week works on both: the beliefs behind the wanting, and the moments that set it off.

statements.text: I could stop any time I wanted to.
statements.verdict: Nicotine makes stopping harder than it sounds.
statements.explanation: It's natural to feel in control, especially on a day when you're not trying to stop. But most quit attempts are made without any help, and very few of those last: in one review, only about 3–5% lasted six to twelve months. That isn't a judgment on anyone's strength. It shows how strongly nicotine pulls, and why understanding, skills and support make a real difference.
statements.source: Hughes, Keely & Naud, 2004; Babb et al., 2017

statements.text: Most people who smoke want to quit.
statements.verdict: About two in three adults who smoke want to.
statements.explanation: In a large US survey, 68% of adults who smoke said they wanted to stop completely. So if part of you wants out while you're still using, you're not unusual or inconsistent. Wanting to stop and still reaching for the next one is exactly how nicotine works. {s: You're in good company. | v: That survey asked about cigarettes, and there's less data on vaping so far, but you're in good company. | p: That survey asked about cigarettes, and there's less data on pouches so far, but you're in good company.}

statements.text: It hasn't harmed me yet, so I'm fine.
statements.verdict: {s: Harm builds quietly. So does recovery. | v: The long-term picture isn't known yet. | p: The long-term picture isn't known yet.}

explanation.smoking: Most of the harm from smoking builds slowly over years, which is why people often feel fine for a long time. The hopeful side works the same way. Your heart rate and blood pressure start to come down within minutes of your last cigarette, and quitting at any age adds years of life, more the earlier you stop. You don't need to feel unwell to have a good reason.
explanation.vaping: Vapes haven't been around long enough for anyone to know the long-term picture. Most of the harm from tobacco comes from the smoke, so the risks are likely to be different. But the nicotine still keeps you dependent: the gap every hour or two, the money, the planning around the next one. You don't need to feel unwell to have a good reason to be free of that.
explanation.pouches: Pouches haven't been around long enough for anyone to know the long-term picture. Most of the harm from tobacco comes from the smoke, so the risks are likely to be different. But the nicotine still keeps you dependent: the gap every hour or two, the money, the planning around the next one. You don't need to feel unwell to have a good reason to be free of that.

source.smoking: Doll et al., 2004; American Cancer Society

chapters.title: Settle in
chapters.text:
[softly] Hi again. Before we start, find somewhere you can be still for a few minutes. Sit back, or lie down if you'd like. [pause]

Take one slow breath in through your nose, and let it go, a little longer on the way out. [long pause]

Let your shoulders drop a little. Let your jaw soften. There's nothing you need to do for the next few minutes except listen.

This morning I asked you to keep using as normal, and to watch. However that went, you've come back for the second half of the day. That counts for more than you might think.

chapters.title: What you noticed
chapters.text:
Let's look back. Your check-ins may be on the screen in front of you. Or you can simply remember. [pause]

Maybe the gap was easy to find. A restless edge in your chest. A fidget in your hands. A sense that the moment wasn't quite finished until you'd {s: lit up | v: had a hit | p: put one in}. If so, you've just seen something that's easy to miss for years. [pause] And if most of your ratings were high, if most of them felt like the gap, that isn't bad news. It means the thing you've been reaching for is mostly fixing a feeling it caused. That's something you can step out of.

Maybe it was harder to find. That's useful too. The gap is quiet. It sits in the background, like that dripping faucet, and you've lived with it for so long it feels like part of the furniture. Often you only notice it in the moment it stops, in those first few {s: seconds | v: seconds | p: minutes} after you use.

Maybe some of them felt like real enjoyment, not relief at all. That's fine. Hold on to that. In a couple of days we'll look at enjoyment closely, with real curiosity, and not to argue you out of anything.

And maybe you forgot to check in at all. [light laugh] That's worth noticing too. The fact that a {s: cigarette | v: vape | p: pouch} can come and go without you really clocking it tells you something. Tomorrow is all about that. The autopilot.

Whatever you found, there's no score here. The only aim today was to look.

chapters.title: Two minds
chapters.text:
[gently] There's something else that often shows up on the first day, and I want to name it.

Part of you wants to stop. That's why you're here. And part of you doesn't, or isn't sure, or feels a small knot of worry at the thought of life without it. [pause]

Both parts make sense. Mixed feelings aren't a sign that you're not ready. They're what it feels like to be in the middle of changing something that's been with you for a long time. They're normal.

Here's something worth knowing about that worry. A lot of it comes from the addiction itself. The same drug that opens the gap every hour or two also makes the thought of never closing it again feel alarming. So the fear isn't proof that you need it. It's one more part of the pull. [pause]

When thoughts like "I could never" or "I'll be miserable" show up this week, you don't have to argue with them. Just notice them. You could even say, quietly, "I'm having the thought that I could never." A thought is something passing through. It isn't a forecast, and it isn't an order. You can let it be there, and still choose what you do next.

chapters.title: Your reason
chapters.text:
Earlier today you chose the reason that matters most to you. Bring it to mind now. [pause]

Not as a rule you have to live up to. More like a direction. A compass doesn't push you anywhere. It just shows you which way is north.

Picture one specific moment your reason points to. Somewhere you'd be. Someone you'd be with. What you'd be doing. Maybe it's keeping up with someone you love, without stopping to catch your breath. Maybe it's waking up without the tug. Maybe it's something only you know. [long pause]

Notice how that moment feels. [pause] That's what this week is about. Not giving something up. Moving toward something you want. Whenever this week gets confusing, or the doubt gets loud, come back to that picture. It'll be waiting.

chapters.title: Tonight
chapters.text:
For the rest of this evening, carry on as normal. If you use before bed, you might notice the gap one more time: the restless edge, and then the settling. Just notice it. There's nothing to fix.

Then sleep. Tomorrow morning, you'll wake up after a long stretch without nicotine, which means you'll wake up in the gap. [pause] Don't change anything. Just notice the first one of the day, and what comes right before it. Tomorrow we'll look at why that one feels so strong, and how so many of them happen without you deciding at all.

Before you go, one more slow breath. In through your nose. [pause] And a long, easy breath out. [long pause]

If you'd like, play this morning's track again tomorrow, or any time. Hearing an idea twice helps it settle.

[warmly] You've done your first day. You looked. That's the beginning of seeing it clearly. Sleep well.

deck.title: The autopilot
deck.intro: Yesterday you watched the gap. Today, what sets it off.

script.voice: warm and clear, a touch brighter than yesterday's morning track; curious rather than instructive, steady pace, slowing for the questions in chapter 1 and the naming practice in chapter 4.

chapters.title: Who decided?
chapters.text:
[warmly] Good morning. Before anything else, a quick question. [pause]

Yesterday, how many times did you really decide to {s: smoke | v: vape | p: have a pouch}? Not just do it. Decide. A clear moment where you thought, "Yes, I want one now," and then reached for it. [long pause]

If you're like most people, the honest answer is: not many. Most of the time, the {s: cigarette was already lit | v: vape was already in your hand | p: pouch was already in} before any thought arrived. The coffee was poured, you stepped outside, the meal ended, the car started, and there it was. Sometimes you only noticed halfway through. Sometimes you reached for {s: the pack | v: your vape | p: the can} and realized you'd had one just a few minutes before.

That's the autopilot. And it isn't a sign that you're careless or that you don't care. It's a sign that your brain has learned something very well. Today we're going to look at how it got built, and why simply seeing it is the first step to switching it off.

chapters.title: How a cue gets wired
chapters.text:
Your brain is a brilliant learner. It notices what happens together, and it links them. [pause]

Say you {s: smoke | v: vape | p: have a pouch} with your morning coffee. The coffee comes, the gap closes, you feel settled. The next day, same again. And the day after. Over months and years, that happens hundreds, then thousands, of times. Each time, the link between coffee and nicotine gets a little stronger.

After a while, the coffee doesn't just go with it. The coffee starts asking for it. The smell, the warm cup in your hand, that first sip: they become a signal. Your brain says, "This is the moment the gap closes," and the wanting switches on before you've had a single thought about it.

It's a bit like a song you know well. Someone plays the first line, and the next line arrives in your head on its own. You didn't choose to think of it. It was just there. Or think of the light switch in a home you've moved out of. Years later, walking into a dark room somewhere else, your hand can still reach for the wall where it used to be.

That's what a cue is. Coffee. Finishing a meal. Your phone. The car. A drink. A stressful email. Each one got paired with nicotine so many times that it now pulls on the habit by itself. [pause] It isn't a choice you keep making. It's a groove that's been worn in, one repetition at a time.

chapters.title: Why mornings are so strong
chapters.text:
[calmly] The first one of the day often feels like the strongest of all. There are two reasons, and they stack on top of each other. [pause]

First, the gap. You've just been asleep for hours without nicotine, so the level is low. You wake up with the gap at its widest, and the first one has the most to close.

Second, the routine. The morning is usually the most repeated stretch of your day. Wake up, phone, coffee, first one. Same order, same place, every single day. It's the most practiced chain of cues you have. Your hands know the moves before you're properly awake.

So the first one of the day isn't proof that you need it most. It's the biggest gap meeting the best-rehearsed routine. Nothing more mysterious than that. [pause] And that makes the morning a very good place to learn.

chapters.title: Seeing it loosens it
chapters.text:
Here's the hopeful part. The autopilot works best when nobody's watching. [pause]

The moment you notice a cue, something shifts. Instead of coffee leading straight to nicotine, there's a small moment in between. A little space where you can see what's happening. "Ah. There's the coffee cue." [pause]

You don't have to do anything with that space yet. Today, you can still use, exactly as normal. I'm only asking you to see it. When a cue shows up, name it in your head. "That's the after-dinner one." "That's the car." "That's the phone." [pause] Naming it, rather than fighting it, is how you start to step out of the groove. Notice what you feel just before, too. Restless? Bored? Tired? A bit pleased with yourself? You'll map that in a few minutes, and it'll tell you a lot. It's also why you keep using this week. The cues are much easier to see while they're still running.

And here's the part worth holding on to. What was learned can be unlearned. Every link your brain made, it made through repetition. After Day Xero, each time a cue shows up and passes without nicotine, that link gets a little weaker. The cues will still knock for a while. Over the first few weeks, they tend to knock less often, and more quietly.

In a moment, you'll look at which cues run your day, and map your three biggest ones. Then this evening, we'll plan one small experiment for tomorrow morning.

[warmly] For now, keep using as normal. Just catch the cue first.

deck.title: Your triggers, decoded
deck.intro: Your biggest cues, one card each. Tap to see what's really going on.

cards.front: Why does coffee feel unfinished without it?
cards.answer: Because they've been paired thousands of times, often first thing, when the gap is widest. Your brain now treats the cup itself as the signal that nicotine is coming.
cards.deeper: Coffee is usually one of the most repeated pairings there is: same time, same cup, same spot, every day. Each time, nicotine closed the gap while the coffee was in your hand, so the two got wired together. That's why coffee on its own can feel oddly incomplete. The good news is that pairings can be rewired. You don't have to give up coffee. Changing the setting helps: a different mug, a different chair, a short walk with it. So does a plan written as "When I pour my coffee, I'll…". If-then plans like that make follow-through more likely.

cards.front: Why does the one after a meal feel so necessary?
cards.answer: A meal ends, you pause, and it's been a while since the last one. That full, settled feeling and the gap closing arrive together, so they've merged into one.
cards.deeper: The end of a meal is a natural full stop, and nicotine has filled that full stop for a long time. Because you've usually gone a while without while you ate, the gap is open too. So the relief of closing it lands right on top of the pleasant, full feeling of having eaten, and the two get credited to the {s: cigarette | v: vape | p: pouch}. People who don't use finish meals and feel full and done in exactly the same way. What helps is giving the meal a new full stop of your own: stand up, brush your teeth, make a tea, take a short walk.

cards.front: Why do your phone and {product} go together?
cards.answer: Both fill small, empty moments. Idle hands, idle mind, a scroll and a {s: smoke | v: hit | p: pouch}. They've shown up in the same moments so often that one now cues the other.
cards.deeper: Phones and nicotine both slot into the in-between bits of the day: waiting, winding down, a minute with nothing to do. {s: A smoke break often comes with a scroll. | v: A vape can be used while scrolling, almost without noticing. | p: A pouch can sit in while you scroll, almost without noticing.} Because both happen so often, the link builds quickly. Watch for the moment you pick up the phone and see if the urge arrives with it. Small changes help a lot: keep the {product} in a different room from where you scroll, or set the phone down for the first minute of a break.

cards.front: Why does getting in the car make you reach for it?
cards.answer: Hands busy, mind free, the same route at the same time. The car is a private, repeated space, so it's become one of the strongest places for the habit.
cards.deeper: Driving is the same few routes, the same times of day and the same seat, over and over. That makes it a perfect place for a cue to form. The car can also feel like your own space, where nobody minds what you do. When you notice the pull as you start the engine, name it: "That's the car." To help on and after Day Xero, give your hands and mouth something else: water, gum, a podcast you save only for driving. And take {product_plural} and anything that goes with them out of the car before your Quit Day.

cards.front: Why does a drink make it so much harder to say no?
cards.answer: Drinks and nicotine are often paired in social, relaxed moments, and after a drink or two, plans can feel easier to bend. So two pulls arrive at once.
cards.deeper: For many people, a drink and a {s: cigarette | v: vape | p: pouch} go together in the same settings: friends, evenings, celebrations. That's a strong, well-practiced pairing. On top of that, alcohol can loosen the part of you that plans ahead, so "just one" can sound more reasonable after a couple of drinks. None of this means you can never drink again. It means the first few weeks after Day Xero are worth planning: fewer drinks, a different setting, a friend who knows, an exit time. Tonight, just notice how often the two show up together.

cards.front: Why does stress feel like the time you need it most?
cards.answer: Because the gap and stress feel alike: restless, tense, on edge. Using closes the gap, and that can feel like calm, so stress and nicotine get wired together.
cards.deeper: When the gap opens during a stressful moment, you feel both at once and can't tell them apart. Using closes the gap, the edge drops, and it feels as if the stress eased. Research on people who smoke found that stress tends to rise between cigarettes and fall after one, which fits the idea that smoking relieves withdrawal rather than stress itself. So the cue isn't really "stress". It's "stress plus the gap". Two days from now we'll look at this loop properly, and at what actually helps in a hard moment.

deck.title: Habits and helpers
deck.intro: Five beliefs about the moments that come with nicotine. Tap Myth or Fact.

statements.text: Coffee and {product_plural} just go together.
statements.verdict: They go together because you've paired them.
statements.explanation: It can feel like a natural match, but nothing in coffee needs nicotine. You've had them together so often that your brain now links them, and the cup itself sets off the wanting. People who don't use drink coffee and enjoy it fully. A pairing that was learned can be relearned: a different mug, a different spot, or a short if-then plan for the first cup all help loosen it.

statements.text: {s: Smoking | v: Vaping | p: A pouch} helps me concentrate.
statements.verdict: It fixes the poor focus the gap causes.
statements.explanation: It feels true because focus often sharpens right after you use. But as nicotine wears off, the gap makes it harder to settle and concentrate. Using brings you back to your normal level, so it feels like a boost. Difficulty concentrating is a known withdrawal symptom, and it tends to ease within two to four weeks of stopping. After that, the dips that come between doses are gone.

statements.text: {s: A cigarette | v: Vaping | p: A pouch} after a meal helps my digestion.
statements.verdict: The meal is done either way. The gap isn't.
statements.explanation: The after-meal one feels like it settles things, but most of that feeling is the gap closing right as you sit back, full and relaxed. People who don't use digest their meals perfectly well, and feel just as done. If meals feel unfinished for a while after Day Xero, that's the old pairing, not your stomach. Give the meal a new ending of your own: stand up, make a tea, take a short walk.

text.smoking: Coffee will hit harder after I quit.
text.vaping: Coffee will hit harder after I quit vaping.
text.pouches: Coffee will hit harder after I quit pouches.

verdict.smoking: True. Plan to cut your coffee back a bit.
verdict.vaping: Unlikely. That finding was about smoke.
verdict.pouches: Unlikely. That finding was about smoke.

explanation.smoking: This one is real. Tobacco smoke makes your body clear caffeine faster. When you stop smoking, the same number of cups can leave a lot more caffeine in your blood. That can feel like jitters, poor sleep or restlessness, which is easy to mistake for cravings. Try cutting back or switching some cups to decaf in your first weeks.
explanation.vaping: The study behind this was about people who stopped smoking. It's the smoke that speeds up how fast the body clears caffeine, so stopping vaping isn't expected to change your coffee much. What may change is the habit: coffee might feel strange without a vape for a while. That's the pairing, and it fades as you practice.
explanation.pouches: The study behind this was about people who stopped smoking. It's the smoke that speeds up how fast the body clears caffeine, so stopping pouches isn't expected to change your coffee much. What may change is the habit: coffee might feel strange without a pouch for a while. That's the pairing, and it fades as you practice.

statements.text: You can't break a habit you've had for years.
statements.verdict: Long habits can change. Millions have done it.
statements.explanation: A long habit can feel like part of who you are, but the links behind it were learned one repetition at a time, and they can weaken the same way. In the US, more than half of adults who have ever smoked have now quit, many after decades. What helps most is seeing the cues, having a plan for each one, and riding out the urges until they fade.

chapters.title: Why one small wait
chapters.text:
[softly] Hi. Let's take a few minutes to get ready for tomorrow morning. [pause]

You've chosen a moment, and a short wait after it. Five minutes, or fifteen, before your first {s: cigarette | v: vape | p: pouch} of the day. I want to explain why something this small matters so much.

If you're like a lot of people who use nicotine, you've rarely, if ever, watched an urge pass. Think about it. The urge shows up, and within moments it's dealt with. You close the gap every time, so you never get to see what the urge does on its own. [pause] Tomorrow, you will. And that one sight matters more than it sounds. Once you've seen an urge come and go on its own, even once, it's hard to fully believe again that you have to answer every single one.

This isn't a test of strength, and it isn't the start of quitting. You can still use as normal tomorrow. It's an experiment with one question: what happens to the urge if I don't answer it straight away?

chapters.title: What it might feel like
chapters.text:
Let me be honest about what you might notice. [pause]

The pull will probably show up right on cue. A restlessness. Maybe a thought like, "Just have it, what's the point?" Maybe your hands will want something to do. It may feel stronger than you expect, or much weaker. Both are useful to know. You might also feel a little silly, standing in the kitchen watching the clock. That's fine too. Curiosity often feels a bit odd at first.

If it rises, notice that it rises. And keep watching. Urges tend to build, peak, and then ease off, a bit like a wave. [pause] You might find it eases sooner than you thought. You might not. Either way, you've learned something about how it moves.

And if you don't make the full time, that's fine. Whatever you manage counts. Two minutes of watching teaches you more than a day of not looking. And if you forget completely, and only notice once the {s: cigarette's lit | v: vape's in your hand | p: pouch is in}, that's the autopilot showing you just how fast it runs. Make a note of it, and try again the next morning.

chapters.title: Rehearse the morning
chapters.text:
[slowly] Let's walk through it now, so your brain has seen it once already. Close your eyes if you'd like. [pause]

Picture waking up tomorrow. The room. The light. How you feel. [pause]

Now picture your moment arriving. Maybe it's your feet touching the floor. Maybe it's the first coffee in your hand. Maybe it's the commute, or picking up your phone. [long pause]

Notice the pull. And name it, quietly: "There's the morning cue." [pause]

Feel where it shows up in your body. The chest. The hands. The mouth. Just notice it, the way you did yesterday with the gap. [pause]

Now see yourself doing the thing you picked for those minutes. A glass of water. A shower. Stepping outside. Or just letting the feeling be there, without doing anything about it. [long pause]

And then, when the time's up, you can use if you want to. If you do, notice that first one. [pause] What was it like, after waiting?

chapters.title: Tonight
chapters.text:
That's the plan. One moment, one short wait, and some curiosity. [pause]

When you're done, log how long you managed in the app, even if it was less than you hoped. It all helps you see the pattern. Tomorrow we'll go one step further, and look closely at what using actually feels like, moment by moment, with fresh eyes.

For now, let today go. You mapped your autopilot and named your cues. You know more about your habit tonight than you did this morning. [pause]

If your mind starts running ahead to the morning, that's okay. Take one slow breath, a little longer on the way out, and let the plan rest. It'll be there when you wake up.

[warmly] Sleep well. I'll see you in the morning.

chapters.title: Where we are
chapters.text:
[warmly] Welcome back. This is day three.

So far you've done two things. You've started to notice the gap: that restless, slightly on-edge feeling that builds between doses. And yesterday you looked at the autopilot, and maybe tried a small wait before your first one of the morning.

However that went, it counts. If you waited fifteen minutes, you learned something. If you didn't wait at all, you learned something too. Nothing this week is a test.

[pause]

Today is a little different. It isn't about waiting, or cutting down. You'll keep using exactly as you normally do. What changes is how you look. Today is about curiosity.

chapters.title: What attention does
chapters.text:
Some years ago, a research team ran a study with people who smoked and wanted to stop. One group joined a well-established quit program, the standard kind. The other group learned something simpler. They practiced paying close attention, to their cravings and to smoking itself. Not fighting it. Not feeling bad about it. Just noticing, with real curiosity, what was actually going on.

The group that learned to pay attention did better than the group on the standard program.

[pause]

Why would that work? Here's how I think about it.

Your brain keeps a kind of summary of nicotine. It wrote that summary a long time ago, and it rarely checks it. The summary says something like: this helps, this feels good, I need this. And because most uses happen on autopilot, with your attention on your phone, or a conversation, or the next thing on your list, the summary almost never gets tested.

So you end up reaching for a memory of how it feels, more than for how it actually feels today.

Attention is how the summary gets checked. When you really look, your brain gets fresh information. And fresh information is hard to argue with.

chapters.title: The story and the experience
chapters.text:
[calmly] Let's try something. Think of the one you'd call your favorite. For a lot of people it's the first one with a morning coffee, or the one after a long stretch of work.

Now notice what your mind says about it. Maybe, that one's really good. That one's my moment. That's the story. A story is made of beliefs, and beliefs are made of words.

[pause]

The experience is something else. The experience is what's actually there, moment by moment. {s: The taste of the smoke on your tongue. The heat at the back of your throat. | v: The taste of the vapor, and how quickly it fades. The scratch at the back of your throat. | p: The taste as the pouch goes in. The tingle, or the burn, on your gum.} The small lift in your head. How long that lift really lasts. And what your mind does next, which is often to start thinking about the next one.

Here's what many people find once they look. Most of what feels good is the restlessness stopping. The gap closing. That relief is real, and I'm not going to tell you it isn't. But it's relief from something nicotine set up in the first place.

Someone who doesn't use nicotine doesn't have that gap, so they don't need anything to close it. They aren't holding back from something good. They're simply where you are in the few minutes after you've used, most of the time, without doing anything.

chapters.title: Curiosity, not judgment
chapters.text:
[gently] Now, an important part. Curiosity is not the same as trying to make it disgusting.

You don't need to hate nicotine to stop. And you don't need to pretend. If you look closely and some part of it feels good, notice that too. Honest beats harsh. The point is to see it as it is. Not as the old story says, and not as some new story says either.

Some thoughts will show up while you look. This is pointless. Leave this one alone, I like it. What if I can't do this. You don't have to argue with any of them. Try putting a few words in front: I'm having the thought that this is pointless.

[pause]

Thoughts are not orders. You can let them talk while you keep looking.

The question to carry with you today is a simple one. What is this actually like, right now? Not what was it like years ago. Not what will life be like without it. Just, what is it like, right now?

chapters.title: Today
chapters.text:
Here's how today goes. Next, a few cards on the stories most of us tell about nicotine. Then a guided use. I'll talk you through one {s: cigarette | v: vaping session | p: pouch}, start to finish, with your eyes open. You can play it straight away if it's a time you'd use anyway, or save it for later in the day. Please don't add an extra one just for this. Use one you were going to have.

Before you start, you'll say how good you expect it to feel. Afterward, you'll say how good it actually was. If there's a difference, it's worth knowing.

[pause]

You don't have to decide anything today. You don't have to believe anything new. Just look.

[warmly] I'll see you in the cards.

deck.title: The stories we tell
deck.intro: Four things most of us say about nicotine. Tap each one and look at it with fresh eyes.

cards.front: Isn't it the {s: taste | v: flavor | p: taste} I enjoy?
cards.answer: Some of it may be pleasant. But ask yourself: would a nicotine-free version do just as well? If the answer is no, the {s: taste | v: flavor | p: taste} is the wrapping. The nicotine is what you're reaching for.
cards.deeper: {s: Think back to your very first cigarette. How did it taste then? For many of us, it took a while to get used to. | v: Think about how many flavors you've tried, and how they all start to taste the same after a while. | p: Think about how the flavor fades within minutes, while the pouch stays in.} Over time, the {s: taste | v: flavor | p: taste} got linked with something else: the gap closing soon after. Your brain paired the two, so now the {s: taste | v: flavor | p: taste} itself feels like a promise of relief. That's why it can seem so good when you've waited a while, and so ordinary when you've just had one. Today, try asking two questions at once: what am I tasting, and what am I waiting for? Notice which one matters more to you right now.

cards.answer: The reward is real: a pause, a moment that's yours, a sense that something's done. Nicotine got attached to it. You can keep the moment and choose what goes in it.
cards.deeper: Look at what you're rewarding yourself with. Usually it's a few things at once: stopping, a change of scene, a moment that belongs to nobody else, a small "well done". Those are worth having. Nicotine came along with them, and it brings something else too: the gap comes back an hour or two later, so each reward quietly sets up the next need. People who don't use still reward themselves, with a coffee outside, a walk, a song, a call to a friend, five minutes doing nothing at all. When you stop, you don't lose the finish line. You get to decide what's waiting there.

cards.answer: Breaks are some of the best minutes in a day: time away, some air, maybe a chat. Nicotine came with the break, but it was never the break itself.
cards.deeper: A good break does three things. It stops the work, it changes the scene, and it gives you permission to breathe. {s: A smoking break also comes with something people rarely notice: a run of long, deep breaths in and slow breaths out. That breathing is calming on its own, and tomorrow you'll learn a version of it you can use anywhere. | v: A vape break often comes with long, slow breaths out, and that breathing is calming on its own. Tomorrow you'll learn a version of it you can use anywhere. | p: With pouches, there often isn't a break at all. The pouch goes in at your desk and you keep working. So the "break" is mostly the gap closing while nothing else changes. Worth noticing today.} Try this today: on your next break, notice which of those three you're actually enjoying. Then ask whether you'd still want the break if there were no {product} in it. If the answer is yes, the break is the part worth keeping. You're allowed breaks without nicotine. Plan to keep yours.

cards.front: Isn't it just who I am?
cards.answer: You weren't born using. You learned it, and part of you has wanted to stop for a while, which is why you're here. That part is you too.
cards.deeper: Nicotine can feel woven into who you are: the friends you {s: smoke | v: vape | p: share a tin} with, the way you handle a hard day, even how you see yourself. That's normal after years of repetition. But identity has room for more than one thing. In a large US survey, about two in three adults who smoked said they wanted to quit. Wanting out is common. It may be the most ordinary thing about you. On Day Xero you won't be someone who uses and can't. You'll be someone who doesn't need to. The friends, the humor and the way you look after people all stay.

chapters.title: Before you start
chapters.text:
[warmly] Hi. If now is a time you'd use anyway, stay with me. If it isn't, that's completely fine. Stop here, and come back later today, when you'd be reaching for one regardless. I'll be right here. And if you're driving, please save this for later too.

[pause]

One more thing before we begin. Please don't have an extra one for this. Use one you were going to have.

If you're ready, find somewhere you can be for a few minutes. Outside is fine. Put your phone down, screen down if you can. You only need to hear me. Have your {s: cigarette and lighter | v: vape | p: tin of pouches} with you, but don't start yet.

[long pause]

You've just said how good you expect this to feel. Keep that number somewhere in the back of your mind. We'll come back to it at the end.

chapters.title: The moment before
chapters.text:
[calmly] Let's start before the first {s: puff | v: hit | p: taste}. This is the part we almost never notice.

Is there a wanting right now? Where is it? Maybe it's in your chest, or your hands, or your mouth. Maybe it's a kind of restlessness, a sense that something isn't quite settled.

[pause]

That's the gap. Just notice how it feels. You don't have to do anything about it for a few more seconds.

Notice, too, what your mind is saying. Maybe, finally. Or, come on. Or nothing at all. Whatever it is, let it be there.

And notice your breathing for a moment. Is it quick, or slow? High in your chest, or low? You don't need to change it. Just see where it is before you start.

[pause]

Now look at the {s: cigarette | v: vape | p: pouch} itself. {s: Notice its weight, the paper, the smell of it before it's lit. | v: Notice its weight, the shape of it, the mouthpiece. | p: Notice the tin, the small white pouch, the smell when you open the lid.} Just look at it, as if you'd never seen one before.

chapters.title: The first one
chapters.text:
{s: Okay. Light it, and take your first puff, slowly, the way you normally would. | v: Okay. Take your first hit, slowly, the way you normally would. | p: Okay. Put the pouch in, where you usually put it.}

[long pause]

What's the taste, right now? Not the taste you expect. The taste that's actually there. {s: Notice the smoke on your tongue, and the heat as it goes down. | v: Notice the flavor, and then notice the vapor itself, underneath the flavor. | p: Notice the flavor, and the tingle or burn starting on your gum.} Is it pleasant? Neutral? Harsh? Any answer is fine.

[pause]

Now your body. {s: Your throat. Your chest as the smoke goes in, and as it comes out. | v: Your throat. Your chest as you breathe in, and as you breathe out. | p: Your gum and your lip. The saliva building. Your heartbeat.} Just notice. You're not looking for anything in particular.

[pause]

And now the part you've been waiting for. {s: Over the next few puffs, | v: Over the next few hits, | p: Over the next few minutes, as it builds,} notice what happens to the restless feeling from a minute ago. Does it ease?

[pause]

Ask yourself, gently: is something good being added here, or is something uncomfortable stopping? Maybe it's a bit of both. Just see.

chapters.title: Keep going, keep noticing
chapters.text:
{s: Keep smoking at your normal pace. | v: Keep going at your normal pace, as many hits as you'd usually take. | p: Leave it where it is, as you normally would.} I'll go quiet for a few moments. Each time I come back, notice one thing.

[long pause]

{s: Is this puff like the first one? Better, worse, or about the same? | v: Is this hit like the first one? Better, worse, or about the same? | p: Is the taste the same as when it went in? Stronger, weaker, or about the same?}

[long pause]

Where's your attention gone? If it's drifted off to a plan, or a worry, or the phone you put down, that's what usually happens. That's the autopilot. No problem. Just come back.

[pause]

You might notice some thoughts. I like this. Or, this is silly. Or, what am I even doing. Let them be thoughts. You can say to yourself, I'm having the thought that this is silly, and let it pass, like a car going by on the street. You don't have to follow it.

[long pause]

Now notice your hands for a moment. {s: What are they doing between puffs? | v: What are they doing between hits? | p: What are they doing, now that the pouch is in?} Is that part of what you like, having something to do?

[pause]

Here's a question worth sitting with. When did the good part peak? Was it near the start? Has it stayed with you, or has it already faded into just doing it?

chapters.title: After
chapters.text:
{s: When you're ready, finish it and put it out. | v: When you'd normally stop, put the vape down. | p: You'll keep the pouch in for a while yet, as long as you normally do. We'll finish our part now, and you can notice the rest on your own.}

[long pause]

Now notice what's left. {s: The taste in your mouth. The smell on your fingers, and maybe your clothes. | v: The taste in your mouth. The sweetness, or the dryness. | p: The taste fading. The feeling on your gum.} How does your body feel now, compared with a few minutes ago?

[pause]

And the restless feeling from the start. Has it gone quiet? That quiet is what you were after. Someone who doesn't use has it most of the day, without doing anything at all.

[pause]

And notice your mind. Is it calm and done, or is part of it already filing away when the next one will be?

[pause]

Last thing. How good was that, really, compared with what you expected? Don't answer yet. Just notice whether there's a difference.

[pause]

[warmly] Whatever you noticed is useful. If you liked parts of it, that's honest, and honest is exactly what we want. There's nothing to decide right now. When you're ready, the next step asks you a few quick questions about what you saw.

Thank you for looking.

deck.title: Pleasure
deck.intro: Five things people believe about the good part. Myth or fact? Go with your gut.

statements.text: Nicotine makes you feel good.
statements.verdict: Partly. Mostly, it ends a bad feeling it started.
statements.explanation: Nicotine does act on the brain's reward system and can bring a small lift. But it wears off fast, and regular users feel restless and on edge as it does. A big part of what feels good is that feeling stopping: the gap closing. That's why it often feels best when you've waited longest, and why the lift fades so quickly once the level is back.

statements.text: People who don't use nicotine are missing out.
statements.verdict: Myth. They don't have a gap to close.

explanation.smoking: Research on mood across the day found that people who smoke tend to feel more tense as each cigarette wears off. Using brings them back to about where non-smokers are most of the time. So the lift is largely a return to normal, and non-users are already there without doing anything. They aren't holding back from something good. They just aren't on the up-and-down.
explanation.vaping: Research on mood across the day found that people who smoke tend to feel more tense as each cigarette wears off. Using brings them back to about where non-smokers are most of the time. So the lift is largely a return to normal, and non-users are already there without doing anything. They aren't holding back from something good. They just aren't on the up-and-down. The up-and-down between doses comes from nicotine itself.
explanation.pouches: Research on mood across the day found that people who smoke tend to feel more tense as each cigarette wears off. Using brings them back to about where non-smokers are most of the time. So the lift is largely a return to normal, and non-users are already there without doing anything. They aren't holding back from something good. They just aren't on the up-and-down. The up-and-down between doses comes from nicotine itself.

statements.text: The first {s: puff | v: hit | p: few minutes of a pouch} is the best part.
statements.verdict: Fact. That's the moment the gap closes.
statements.explanation: The first one arrives when your nicotine level is lowest and the gap is widest, so it's the biggest change you'll feel. After that, you're mostly topping up a level that's already back. Your body also gets used to nicotine over the course of a day, which is part of why the first one of the morning tends to feel strongest. If you noticed the good part was early and short, this is why.

statements.text: I'll never enjoy a party again.
statements.verdict: Myth. The pull fades. The party stays.
statements.explanation: Early on, a party can bring strong urges, because your brain has learned to link the two. That's worth planning for. But cravings become less frequent over the first weeks after quitting. And on average, people who quit smoking report better mood and quality of life, not worse. The music, the people and the conversation were always the good part. They're still there.

statements.text: Rewards need nicotine.
statements.verdict: Myth. The reward is the moment, not the nicotine.
statements.explanation: Think about what you're really rewarding yourself with: a pause, some air, the sense that something's done. Those stay. Nicotine adds a hidden cost. About half of it is gone from your body in around two hours, and as it goes the gap comes back, so each reward quietly sets up the next need. Non-users still have treats, breaks and finish lines. You get to choose what goes in yours.

deck.title: Why it feels like it calms you

script.voice: Calm, steady and kind, a touch slower than usual; plain-spoken and confident when explaining the loop, softer and more reassuring in chapter 4.

chapters.title: The moment it seems to work
chapters.text:
[warmly] Welcome to day four.

I'd like you to think of the last time stress really hit. Maybe a tense message at work. An argument. Running late, with everything going wrong at once.

[pause]

Got one?

What did you reach for?

For a lot of people, the answer is nicotine. And it seemed to work. {s: You stepped outside, lit up, and a minute later the edge had come off. | v: You took a few hits, and a minute later the edge had come off. | p: You put a pouch in, and a few minutes later the edge had come off.}

I'm not going to tell you that didn't happen. The relief was real. Today we're going to look at what, exactly, it relieved. Because once you've seen it, it's very hard to unsee.

chapters.title: The loop
chapters.text:
A researcher who studies stress looked closely at this question: does smoking really calm people down? What the evidence showed was a pattern. People who smoke tend to feel a little more stressed, overall, than people who don't. Their tension rises between cigarettes, as the nicotine wears off. Smoking brings it back down, to about where a non-smoker is most of the time. And then it starts to rise again.

[pause]

So the calm that follows is real. But it's mostly a return to normal. It's the gap closing.

Nicotine doesn't stay with you for long. About half of it is gone from your body in around two hours. So through the day, you ride a small up and down that a non-user doesn't have. Down a little, top up. Down a little, top up.

Now add real stress on top. The email, the bill, the argument. Stress plus the gap feels like a lot. You use, the gap closes, and the total drops. It feels as if nicotine dealt with the stress.

But look at what's still there. The email. The bill. The argument. Nothing about the actual problem has changed. Only the gap has.

chapters.title: Why they feel the same
chapters.text:
[calmly] Here's why it's so convincing. The gap and stress feel very alike in the body.

Both can make your chest feel tight. Both make it hard to settle. Both shorten your fuse, and both set your thoughts racing a little. So when they show up together, it's almost impossible to tell which is which.

And your brain learns a simple rule. Stress, then nicotine, then relief. Every time it seems to work, the rule gets a little stronger. That's the loop.

There's one more twist. On a hard day, you might find yourself reaching for it more often. And more uses means more gaps through the day. So the days you most want calm can end up with the most ups and downs built in.

[pause]

None of this is a flaw in you. It's simply how nicotine works for anyone who uses it regularly. And it means something hopeful. If part of your everyday stress is the gap, then that part can go.

chapters.title: What happens after people stop
chapters.text:
That isn't just a theory. A large review of studies, published in the BMJ, looked at people's mental health after they stopped smoking. On average, the people who quit ended up with lower anxiety, lower stress and less depression than the people who kept smoking. Their mood and their quality of life tended to go up, not down.

[pause]

[reassuring] I want to be honest about the first part, though. In the first days and weeks after stopping, many people feel restless, irritable or on edge. That's withdrawal, and it's real. It usually peaks in the first week and eases over two to four weeks. You'll have tools for it, and a plan, and you won't be doing it on your own.

But the longer picture runs the other way from what most people fear. Stopping tends to lower stress, not raise it.

{s: Most of this research was with people who smoked, so it speaks directly to you. | v: Most of this research was with people who smoked. The up and down between doses comes from the nicotine itself, so it's worth watching for in your own day. | p: Most of this research was with people who smoked. The up and down between doses comes from the nicotine itself, so it's worth watching for in your own day.}

chapters.title: Keep the break
chapters.text:
[gently] So what was helping, all those times?

Some of it was the gap closing. But some of it was everything that came along with it. {s: Stepping away. A change of air. And, if you think about it, the breathing: a long, deep breath in, and a slow breath out, again and again. | v: Stepping away. And, if you think about it, the breathing: a deep breath in, and a long, slow breath out, again and again. | p: Taking a second for yourself. A small pause in the middle of everything.}

You can keep all of that. You need breaks when things get hard. Everyone does. You can keep the break, and leave the nicotine out of it.

Next, I'll show you a breath you can use in the moment, anywhere, in about thirty seconds. Then a few cards about stress, and a plan for the two moments that get to you most.

For today, keep using as you normally do. Just one thing. When stress hits, notice it, and ask: is this the situation, the gap, or both?

[pause]

You don't need to fix it. Just see which is which.

deck.title: A breath that works in the moment

beats.title: Two in, one long out
beats.body:
Breathe in through your nose. At the top, take one more short sip of air. Then breathe out slowly through your mouth, for as long as is comfortable. That's one sigh.

In a study of daily breathing practice, this pattern improved mood and calmed the body. Source: Balban et al., 2023

Feeling light-headed? Breathe normally for a moment, then rejoin when you're ready.

deck.title: What stress actually is
deck.intro: Four questions about stress, and what's really going on. Tap each card.

cards.front: Is it stress, or is it the gap?
cards.answer: Often both at once. Stress comes from what's happening around you. The gap comes from nicotine wearing off. They feel alike, so each gets blamed on the other.
cards.deeper: Stress is your body gearing up for something: a deadline, a hard conversation, a problem to fix. The gap is the restless, slightly empty feeling as nicotine wears off between doses. Both can tighten your chest and shorten your fuse. Here's a quick way to tell them apart. Ask yourself: would this feeling be here if nothing had gone wrong today? If it shows up on a calm afternoon, around when your last one would be wearing off, that's mostly the gap. If it's tied to something real, it's stress, and the gap may be adding to it. Today, just try naming which is which.

cards.front: Why do hard days feel harder when you use?
cards.answer: On a hard day you may reach for it more often, and every use brings another gap. So the worst days can carry the most extra ups and downs.
cards.deeper: Picture an ordinary day: a few gaps, each one closed. Now picture a bad day. There's more stress, so you reach for it more, and the gaps come around faster. Each one adds a little restlessness on top of the real problem. When researchers looked at this, they found that people who smoke tend to feel slightly more stressed overall than people who don't, and that tension rises between cigarettes. That doesn't mean your hard days aren't hard. They are. It means part of what makes them so heavy is extra weight you won't have to carry once you've stopped.

cards.front: What actually helps in two minutes?
cards.answer: Something for your body and something for your mind: a few long breaths out, a change of place, a word with someone. Small, quick and there whenever you need it.
cards.deeper: For your body, the sigh you just practiced. In a study at Stanford, people who did five minutes of cyclic sighing a day saw their mood improve and their body calm down. In a tense moment, two or three sighs take about thirty seconds. For your surroundings, step outside, walk to another room, or get a glass of water. A change of scene gives you a minute before you decide anything. For your mind, name it: "this is stress", "this is the gap". Then ask what would actually help with the problem. And for your people, a two-line message to someone who gets it. Pick whichever fits the moment.

cards.front: When is stress more than stress?
cards.answer: When it doesn't lift, keeps you from sleeping or getting through the day, or comes with feeling low or hopeless most days. That's worth talking to someone about.
cards.deeper: Everyday stress rises and falls with what's going on. Sometimes it doesn't fall. Worry runs all day. Panic arrives out of nowhere. You feel low for weeks, or you have thoughts that you'd be better off not here. That isn't a nicotine problem, and it isn't something to push through on your own. It's common, it's nobody's fault, and there's help for it. You can get help with this and still work on quitting. A doctor can help with both. If stress or low mood is getting in the way of everyday life, talk to a doctor or a mental health professional. If you ever feel unsafe, contact a helpline or your local emergency number now.

statements.text: I need it when things go wrong.

statements.explanation: When things go wrong, you do need something: a minute to step back, a breath, someone to talk to. Nicotine has been standing in that spot for so long that it feels like the thing itself. But what it actually relieves is the gap, which rises between doses and adds to the stress you already have. Keep the minute, the breath and the person. They help with the problem.

statements.text: People who quit end up happier, on average.
statements.verdict: Fact, on average, once the first weeks pass.
statements.explanation: A large review in the BMJ brought together studies that followed people who quit smoking and people who kept going. On average, those who quit had lower anxiety, depression and stress afterward, and better mood and quality of life. These studies show a link, not a guarantee for any one person, and the first weeks can be bumpy. But the common fear, that quitting means a duller, more stressed life, isn't what the evidence shows.

statements.text: The irritability from withdrawal is temporary.
statements.verdict: Fact. It peaks early, then eases.
statements.explanation: Irritability, restlessness and trouble concentrating are real withdrawal symptoms. They're usually strongest in the first week and mostly ease within two to four weeks. Knowing that helps. A short fuse on day three isn't who you are now. It's your body adjusting, and it passes. Warning the people around you, and having a plan for the hard moments, makes that stretch easier for everyone.

deck.title: Surfing the urge
deck.intro: A guided practice, about seven minutes. Find somewhere to sit. If you can, have your {product} where you can see it. You won't use it during the track. Still in prep: you can use as normal afterwards if you want to.

script.voice: Slow and grounded, warm, a little lower in energy than the other morning tracks; leave real room in every [long pause]; it's a practice, not a talk.

chapters.title: Why this skill
chapters.text:
[warmly] Welcome to day five. Today is about one skill. If I could only give you one thing to take into Day Xero, it would be this.

Here's what a craving does if you don't act on it. It rises. It peaks. And then it falls. Usually within a few minutes. From the inside, it can feel as if it will keep building until something gives. It won't. It's a wave, and waves break. [pause]

Most of us have never seen that happen. The urge starts to rise, and within seconds we {s: light up | v: take a hit | p: put one in}. So the wave never gets the chance to fall by itself, and we come away believing that only nicotine could have ended it. [pause]

Today you're going to watch one fall. The practice is called urge surfing. In a study with people who smoked, one short session of it led to fewer cigarettes in the week that followed. Not because they fought harder. Because they stopped fighting, and started watching.

chapters.title: Find a wave
chapters.text:
You're still in your prep week, so nothing is being taken away. If you want to use after this, you can. Right now, we're only learning that you don't have to do it straight away. [pause]

Find a place to sit. Feet on the floor. If it's safe to, let your eyes close, or rest them on one spot in front of you. [pause]

Now we need a wave. If you have {s: your cigarettes | v: your vape | p: your tin} nearby, hold {s: the pack | v: it | p: it} in your hand, or put it where you can see it. If it isn't nearby, picture your next one. Where you'll be. The {s: lighter in your hand | v: weight of it in your hand | p: lid coming off}. That first {s: drag | v: pull | p: tingle}. [long pause]

Maybe there's a pull already. Maybe it's faint. Any size is fine. If nothing shows up at all, that's fine too. Practice with whatever restlessness is here, and come back to this track the next time a craving arrives on its own. [pause]

Give it a number from zero to ten. Zero is nothing. Ten is the strongest you've ever felt. Just notice the number. [long pause]

chapters.title: Ride it
chapters.text:
[slowly] Now, instead of doing something about it, let's look at it. [pause]

Where is it in your body? Start at your mouth and throat. Is there a dryness, a tightness, a kind of reaching? [pause] Move down to your chest. Pressure, a flutter, a hollow feeling? [pause] Your stomach. [pause] Your hands. Do they want something to hold? [long pause]

Pick the place where it's strongest. Rest your attention there, the way you'd watch a wave come in from the beach. You don't have to like it. You only have to look. [pause]

Is it sharp or dull? Still, or moving? Does it have edges? Is it growing, shrinking, or staying the same? [long pause]

Now bring your breath to it. In slowly through your nose. And out, a little longer than the in-breath. Imagine the breath going to that spot and making a bit more room around the feeling. You're not pushing it out. You're giving it space. [long pause]

Your mind will probably start talking. Just have one. This is pointless. I can't do this. That's normal. When a thought arrives, name it, quietly. Thinking. Or: there's the thought that I need one. Then come back to the body. [long pause]

Notice what's happening. The craving is asking you to do something, and you're not doing it. And you're still here. Nothing has broken. [pause]

Keep breathing. In through the nose. Long and slow on the way out. [long pause]

Check on the wave. Is it where it was? Has it moved, changed shape, softened at the edges? Sometimes it surges once more before it drops. If it does, ride that too. You're on the board. You don't have to steer the ocean. [long pause]

One more breath, a little slower than the last. [long pause]

Now give it a number again. Zero to ten. [long pause]

chapters.title: What just happened
chapters.text:
[gently] Whatever your number is, something useful happened. [pause]

If it dropped, you've just watched a craving fall without nicotine. That might be the most important thing you learn this week, because part of your brain has believed the opposite for a long time.

If it stayed the same, or even went up, that's useful too. You sat with it for a few minutes and didn't have to obey it. That's the skill. The wave doesn't have to vanish for you to be all right. [pause]

Here's one more thing worth noticing. Part of what made the craving feel big was a quieter feeling underneath it: a worry about life without nicotine. That worry can feel like your own good sense. It isn't. It's part of the trap. The addiction keeps you close by making the way out look frightening. Once you can see that, the fear loosens its grip, and you start to notice that you aren't giving anything up. You're getting out. [pause]

Every wave you ride teaches your brain that a craving is a feeling, not an emergency, and the next one tends to be a little easier.

Today's mission is to do this once more, with a real craving. Open Craving SOS for three minutes before you decide anything. Then rate how high it peaked. That's all.

deck.title: Anatomy of a craving
deck.intro: Four questions about cravings. Tap each card to turn it over.

cards.answer: Usually two things at once: the gap, as your nicotine level drops, and a cue, like coffee, a break or a feeling. Together they switch on the urge before you've decided anything.
cards.deeper: Nicotine doesn't stay in your blood for long, and as the level falls, the gap opens: that restless, slightly-on-edge feeling. On its own it's fairly mild. But your brain has also learned to expect nicotine at certain moments: the first coffee, the end of a meal, getting in the car, a tense email. Each of those is a cue, and a cue can switch on a strong urge even when the gap is small. That's why you can want one right after you've had one, if the moment fits. After Day Xero, most of the nicotine leaves your body within a few days. The cues take longer to unlearn, and every wave you ride teaches them faster.

cards.front: How long does a craving last?
cards.answer: Usually a few minutes. It rises, peaks and passes. From the inside it can feel endless, which is exactly why it helps to know that it has an end.
cards.deeper: Inside a craving, time stretches. A few minutes can feel like an hour, and the mind fills in the rest: this will keep getting worse until I give in. It won't. Each wave rises, peaks and passes, usually within a few minutes. Another may come along later, often when a new cue shows up, but each one is its own wave, and each one ends. That's why Craving SOS counts the time you've ridden: so you can watch the peak go by. Try this today: glance at the clock when a craving starts, and again when you notice it's gone. You may be surprised how short it was.

cards.front: Why does it shrink each time I ride it?
cards.answer: When a craving passes without nicotine, your brain learns that the cue doesn't always bring a dose. The link loosens, so the next wave tends to be smaller.
cards.deeper: Your brain is always predicting. For years, a cue like coffee, the car or stress has been followed by nicotine, so your brain learned to fire up the urge ahead of time, to get you ready. When you ride a craving out, the cue arrives and the dose doesn't. The prediction was wrong, and the brain updates. One ride doesn't erase the link, but it loosens it. Ride enough of them and the waves tend to come less often and break sooner. It's also why one {s: cigarette | v: hit | p: pouch} in the early days after Day Xero matters more than it seems: it teaches the old lesson again.

cards.front: What does the craving voice say?
cards.answer: "Just one." "You deserve it." "Start tomorrow." It sounds like your own reasoning. It's the craving talking, and you don't have to argue with it or obey it.
cards.deeper: The craving voice is convincing because it uses your voice. It rarely says "give me nicotine". It says: you've had a hard day. One won't matter. Start properly on Monday. You'll never manage this anyway, so why suffer? It can even sound kind: you've earned a break. Notice the pattern. However it starts, every line ends in the same place, and that's how you can recognize it. You don't need to win the argument; arguing keeps you in the conversation. Just name it: "There's the craving voice." Or: "I'm having the thought that one won't matter." Then let it talk while you get on with something else.
