beats.title: It came. You stayed.
beats.body:
Whatever your numbers did, you held that feeling for a couple of minutes without doing what it said. That's the skill.

If it eased, you just watched it pass without nicotine. If it stayed the same, it doesn't have to shrink for you to be all right. If it got louder, that's common: paying attention can turn the volume up at first, and it isn't failing. If not much showed up, try it again later, just before your next {product}, when the pull is stronger.

That jolt of panic when you pictured life without it? That's the addiction talking. It isn't your judgment and it isn't a warning. It's part of the trap.

Where you felt it is your early signal. When you feel it there, you'll know a wave is starting. If it's still loud, open Craving SOS for three minutes. It's still your prep week, so after that, the choice is yours.

deck.title: Cravings
deck.intro: Five things people believe about cravings. Myth or fact?

statements.text: If I don't give in, a craving just keeps getting stronger.
statements.verdict: Cravings peak and pass on their own.
statements.explanation: It can feel that way, because most of us answer a craving long before it peaks. Left alone, a craving rises, peaks and passes, usually within a few minutes. In a study of urge surfing, people who learned to watch their urges, rather than fight or obey them, went on to smoke fewer cigarettes. You don't have to make a craving go away. You only have to let it finish.

statements.text: Cravings last for hours.
statements.verdict: One craving lasts minutes, not hours.
statements.explanation: A long, uncomfortable afternoon can feel like one endless craving. Usually it's several shorter waves, each set off by a cue or by the gap, with calmer stretches in between that are easy to miss. Each wave rises, peaks and passes, usually within a few minutes. Spotting the calm stretches matters: it shows you the craving isn't constant, and it gives you room to do something else before the next one.

statements.text: After I quit, one won't hurt.
statements.verdict: Early on, one tends to lead to more.
statements.explanation: This is one of the craving voice's favorite lines. In a study of people quitting with the patch, using at all in the first two weeks strongly predicted going back to regular use. The problem isn't that one {s: cigarette | v: hit | p: pouch} is a disaster. It's that it reopens the gap and reteaches the cue. If a slip does happen, treat it as something to learn from, not a reason to stop trying. The app has a slip plan for exactly that.

statements.text: If I'm still thinking about {s: smoking | v: vaping | p: pouches}, I'm failing.
statements.verdict: Thoughts will come. What you do counts.
statements.explanation: Minds bring up old habits, especially in the places where they used to happen. Thoughts about nicotine will show up after Day Xero, sometimes out of nowhere. Having them isn't failing. The skill is noticing the thought, naming it ("I'm having the thought that I want one") and carrying on with what matters to you. In a large trial, an app built on this approach helped more people quit than a standard quit app.

statements.text: Cravings get less frequent over the first weeks.
statements.verdict: For most people, they ease with time.
statements.explanation: Withdrawal symptoms, cravings included, are usually strongest in the first week, then ease over the following weeks for most people. Cravings tend to come less often and with less force, though a strong cue can still bring one up now and then, even months later. When that happens, it's one wave, not a sign you're back at the start. You ride it the same way.

deck.title: Thoughts are not orders
deck.intro: A short, quiet practice for the evening. About five minutes. Somewhere comfortable is best.

script.voice: Quiet, intimate evening delivery, slower than the morning track, gentle and unhurried; a hint of warmth on the notification image; no lift in energy at the end.

chapters.title: The voice
chapters.text:
[calmly] Good evening. Let's end today with something short and quiet. [pause]

Earlier, while you were surfing, your mind probably had plenty to say. Just one. You deserve it. This is silly. I'll start properly on Monday. That voice doesn't stop because you've decided to quit. In the first days, it may even get louder. So tonight we'll practice a different way of hearing it. [pause]

Here's the idea. A thought is something your mind makes, the way your heart makes a beat. Some thoughts are true and some aren't. Either way, a thought isn't an order. You can hear it without arguing with it, and without doing what it says.

chapters.title: Name it
chapters.text:
Settle in. Let your shoulders drop. [pause]

Bring to mind one thought that tends to show up around nicotine. Maybe, I need one. Maybe, I can't relax without it. Maybe, I'll never manage this. Pick the one that feels most familiar, and say it to yourself the way you usually hear it. [long pause]

Notice how it lands. Does it feel true? Does it tug at you? [pause]

Now say it again, with a few words in front. I'm having the thought that... I need one. [long pause]

And once more, one step further back. I notice I'm having the thought that... I need one. [long pause]

What changed? The words are the same. But now there's a little space between you and them. You're the one hearing the thought. You're not the thought. [pause]

You can use other labels too. There's the craving voice. There's the just-one story. Or simply: thinking. Short and plain is best. The label isn't there to shut the thought up. It's there to remind you which of you is the thought, and which of you is listening. [pause]

chapters.title: Let it be
chapters.text:
Here's another way to picture it. Think of your thoughts as notifications on your phone. They light up the screen. Some are loud. Some keep coming back. You can see them without opening them, and you don't have to reply. [pause]

So the next time just one lights up, you can see it. There it is. The craving notification. And you can carry on with what you were doing. [long pause]

You don't need to make the thought go away. You don't need to win the argument. Arguing with a craving thought is like replying to a notification you don't want: it only brings more of them. Let it sit on the screen. It will scroll away when the next thing comes in. [pause]

And if the same notification keeps coming back, that's fine too. Each time, you see it, you name it, and you carry on. That isn't failing at the practice. That is the practice. [long pause]

chapters.title: Keep going
chapters.text:
[warmly] There's one more piece, and it's the one that matters most. While that thought is on the screen, what do you do? You keep doing what matters to you. [pause]

Think about the reason that brought you here, the one you chose on the first day. Bring it to mind now. [long pause]

That's your direction. Thoughts will come and go along the way, and some will be loud. You can hear every one of them and still keep walking that way. They don't need to be quiet first. [pause]

Think of how many things you've already done while part of you didn't want to. Getting up on a cold morning. A hard conversation. You didn't wait until you felt ready. You did it because it mattered. [pause]

Here's something to try before you sleep, or tomorrow. The next time a nicotine thought shows up, put those words in front of it: I'm having the thought that. Then take one slow breath, and choose what you'll do next. You can still use, if that's what you decide. It's your prep week. The practice is in the choosing. [pause]

Tomorrow we'll set up the world around you, so that choosing gets easier. [pause]

Sleep well.

learned: A craving rises, peaks and passes, usually within a few minutes.
You can feel an urge fully without doing what it says.
“I'm having the thought that…” turns an order back into a thought.

deck.title: You don't have to white-knuckle it

script.voice: Warm, practical and steady, a touch brisker than yesterday; matter-of-fact and reassuring on the NRT section, never salesy; slow down on the safety list and the two medicine names.

chapters.title: Holding on isn't a plan
chapters.text:
[warmly] Hello again. Two days to go until Day Xero, and today is a practical one. [pause]

When most people try to quit, they rely on one thing: holding on. Gritting their teeth through every craving. White-knuckling it. You may know how that goes. On a good morning, holding on can feel easy. But at the end of a long day, when you're tired, or hungry, or stressed, or someone offers you one, holding on gets much harder. [pause]

Scientists still argue about whether willpower really runs out, like a muscle that tires. But you know the feeling. And you don't need to settle the argument to act on it. The plan is simple: make fewer moments depend on willpower in the first place. [pause]

That isn't a shortcut, and it isn't a sign of weakness. It's what you'd do with any hard job. You'd set things up so that the right move is also the easy one.

chapters.title: Your space
chapters.text:
So let's change the setup. Three parts: your space, your people and, if you want it, medicine. [pause]

Start with your space. A lot of nicotine use happens simply because it's right there. {s: The pack in your pocket. The lighter in the car. | v: The vape on the desk. The charger by the bed. | p: The tin in your pocket. The spare in the car.} Each one is a cue, and each one makes using the easiest thing within reach. [pause]

Today you'll move your nicotine to one inconvenient spot. Not hidden away for good. Just out of easy reach. A drawer in another room. A box on a high shelf. Those extra steps won't stop you. They buy a craving time to do what you practiced yesterday: rise, peak and pass. [pause]

And in the places where your nicotine used to live, you'll put your quit kit. Water. Sugar-free gum or mints. Something for your hands. So when your hand reaches for the old spot, it finds something else. [pause]

Then your people. One message today means that on Day Xero, somebody knows, and somebody has your back. You may be surprised how glad people are to be asked. [long pause]

chapters.title: NRT, honestly
chapters.text:
[calmly] Now, nicotine replacement. Some people feel uneasy about it, so let's be clear about what it is. [pause]

Nicotine replacement, or NRT, means patches, gum, lozenges, sprays and inhalers. They give you nicotine as a tested medicine, in measured doses. A patch releases it slowly and steadily through the day, without the ups and downs of {s: cigarette after cigarette | v: hit after hit | p: pouch after pouch}. And the whole plan is built to step down to zero. [pause]

What we've worked on all week takes away the wanting: the belief that nicotine gives you something. NRT works on a different part: the physical edge in the first weeks, while your body adjusts. Different jobs. They work well together. [pause]

And it isn't cheating. A Cochrane review of more than a hundred trials found that people who use NRT are around fifty to sixty percent more likely to quit than people who don't. Another Cochrane review found that a patch plus a faster form, like gum or a lozenge, works better than either one alone. [pause]

If you choose it, a few things matter. You start NRT on Day Xero, the morning you stop {s: smoking | v: vaping | p: using pouches}, not while you're still using. You follow the pack, and the app's NRT plan reminds you of each step. And some people should check with a doctor or pharmacist before starting. [slowly] If you're pregnant or breastfeeding. If you've recently had a heart attack or a stroke, or you have a heart condition. If you take other medicines. Or if you're under eighteen. [pause]

{s: | v: | p: You have one more option, too. If there's time before Day Xero, you can step down your pouch strength first, and the app can plan that with you. [pause]}

Not using NRT is fine too. Plenty of people quit without it. Either choice is a good one, as long as you make it with your eyes open.

chapters.title: Other options
chapters.text:
There are also prescription medicines that help people quit. Two you might hear about are varenicline /vəˈrɛnɪkliːn/ and cytisine /ˈsɪtɪsiːn/. Neither one is nicotine. They act on the same parts of the brain that nicotine does, which can take the edge off cravings and make nicotine feel less rewarding. What's available depends on where you live, and they aren't right for everyone. If you're curious, ask your doctor. [pause]

Today's job is setting up. Next, you'll get a clear picture of NRT, check a few common worries about it, set up your space and choose your people. None of it needs to be perfect. [pause]

[warmly] Here's the thing to hold on to. Making it easy on yourself isn't a sign that you can't do it. It's how hard things get done. You're not relying on a clenched fist. You're arranging your days so the next good choice is the obvious one. [pause]

Let's get you set up.

deck.title: Nicotine replacement, explained
deck.intro: Four things worth knowing about nicotine replacement. Tap each card to turn it over.

cards.answer: Nicotine as a tested medicine: patches, gum, lozenges, sprays and inhalers. A measured dose, {s: no smoke | v: no vape | p: no pouches}, and a plan that steps down to zero.
cards.deeper: NRT has one job: to take the edge off the physical side of stopping while your body adjusts, over a planned number of weeks. It doesn't take away the wanting. That's what this week has been for. Think of them as a team. The understanding you're building means you no longer believe nicotine gives you something. NRT means the restless, on-edge feeling of the first weeks is softer while that understanding settles in. In a review of 133 trials, people using NRT were 50–60% more likely to quit than people who didn't. That's a real boost, not a guarantee, and it works best alongside a plan like this one.

cards.front: Patch or fast-acting: what's the difference?
cards.answer: A patch gives a steady background level all day. Gum, lozenges, sprays and inhalers act faster, and you use them when a craving hits. They do different jobs.
cards.deeper: The patch is the floor. You put a fresh one on each morning and it releases nicotine slowly through your skin, so the gap never opens too wide. Some people keep it on for 24 hours, which helps with cravings first thing. Others take it off at bedtime, which can help with vivid dreams; check your pack says you can. The fast-acting forms handle the waves on top. Gum isn't chewed like ordinary gum: chew slowly until it tingles, park it against your cheek, then chew again. A lozenge dissolves slowly in your mouth. Sprays and inhalers are other fast options. The app's NRT plan covers the patch, gum, lozenge and inhaler.

cards.front: Can I use two kinds together?
cards.answer: Yes. A patch plus a fast-acting form works better than either one alone. Follow both packs, and ask a pharmacist to check the strengths if you're unsure.
cards.deeper: This is called combination NRT. The patch covers the background, and the gum, lozenge, spray or inhaler covers the sudden waves: the first coffee, the drive home, the difficult conversation. A Cochrane review of NRT doses and combinations found that a patch together with a fast-acting form helps more people quit than one form on its own. Follow each pack's instructions. If a label seems to say something different, or you're not sure which strengths to pick, a pharmacist can check it with you in a few minutes. The app's NRT plan then reminds you when to change patches and when each step down is due.

cards.front: Is it safe, and who should check first?
cards.answer: For most adults, NRT used as the pack says is a safe way through withdrawal. A few people should check with a doctor or pharmacist before they start.
cards.deeper: Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, have recently had a heart attack or stroke, have a heart condition, are under 18, or take other regular medicines. That isn't because NRT is off limits; the right choice just depends on your situation. Whatever you use, follow the pack. Side effects are usually mild: a sore mouth or hiccups from gum (often from chewing too fast), or itchy skin under a patch, so put each new patch in a different spot. Some people have vivid dreams with a patch worn overnight. If anything feels wrong, stop and ask a pharmacist.

deck.title: NRT
deck.intro: Five things people say about nicotine replacement. Myth or fact?

statements.text: NRT just swaps one addiction for another.
statements.verdict: It's a short bridge, not a new habit.
statements.explanation: What keeps nicotine use going is fast, repeated doses tied to cues and rituals: the {s: lighter and the break outside | v: hit at your desk | p: tin in your pocket}. NRT is built differently. A patch releases nicotine slowly and steadily, with no ritual attached, and the plan steps down to zero over a set number of weeks. Meanwhile, the work you're doing this week takes away the reasons you wanted nicotine at all. That's a way out, not a swap.

statements.text: Patches don't really work.
statements.verdict: The evidence says they do.
statements.explanation: A Cochrane review of 133 trials found that people using NRT, patches included, were 50–60% more likely to quit than people using a placebo or nothing. That's a boost, not a guarantee: NRT eases the physical side, it doesn't make the decision for you. If a patch didn't help you before, look at how it was used: the strength, how long, whether it was paired with a fast-acting form. Each of those makes a difference.

statements.text: Nicotine is the part that causes cancer.
statements.verdict: Most of the harm comes from smoke.
statements.explanation: Nicotine isn't harmless. It's what makes these products so hard to stop, and it raises your heart rate for a while. But a major report from the Royal College of Physicians concluded that most of the serious harm from smoking, cancer included, comes from the smoke made by burning tobacco, not from the nicotine. That's why medicinal nicotine, used as the pack directs for a planned few weeks, is recommended as a way through withdrawal.

statements.text: Using a patch and gum together is safe and works better.
statements.verdict: Fact, when you follow both packs.
statements.explanation: A Cochrane review found that combining a patch with a fast-acting form, such as gum or a lozenge, helps more people quit than using one form alone. The patch keeps a steady background level, and the fast-acting form handles sudden cravings. Use each one as its pack directs. If you're unsure about strengths, or a label gives you pause, a pharmacist can check it with you in a few minutes.

statements.text: I should keep {s: smoking | v: vaping | p: using pouches} while I start the patch.
statements.verdict: In this plan, NRT starts when you stop.
statements.explanation: In this program you start NRT on Day Xero, the morning you stop, and that's the usual instruction on the pack too. Using both keeps your nicotine level high and keeps the old cues paired with a dose, which is exactly the link Day Xero breaks. Some doctors do use NRT for a short time before a quit date. If that interests you, plan it with your doctor or pharmacist rather than improvising.

script.voice: Warm, steady and unhurried, like a counselor who's on your side; gentle on the fears, plain and confident on the facts, never cheerleading. About 130 words a minute, with real space in the pauses.

chapters.title: The fear, out loud
chapters.text:
[warmly] Tomorrow is Day Xero. And if part of you feels uneasy about that this morning, I'd like to start right there. [pause]

Maybe there's a tightness when you think about tomorrow. A quiet voice saying "not yet." Or a list of reasons this might be a bad week to stop. [pause] That's normal. Almost everyone feels some version of it the day before.

Here's what I'd like you to see. That fear isn't a sign you're not ready. It's one of the ways nicotine keeps people using. Think about it. If stopping felt like nothing, nobody would stay stuck for years. The dread of going without is part of how the addiction protects itself. [pause] So of course it's loud today. Tomorrow is the day it stops being fed.

You don't have to argue with the fear, and you don't have to wait for it to leave. You can just notice it. "There's the fear." [pause] And then look at what it's actually saying.

So let's do that. We'll take the big fears one at a time, with our eyes open.

chapters.title: "I'll miss it"
chapters.text:
The first one usually sounds like this: I'll miss it.

So what, exactly, would you miss? [pause] All week you've been watching closely. You've seen the gap: that restless, slightly empty feeling that builds between doses. And you've seen that most of what feels good about {s: a cigarette | v: the vape | p: a pouch} is that gap closing.

People who don't use nicotine don't have the gap. They don't spend the day topping up a feeling the last dose left behind. So what you'd miss isn't a pleasure they're going without. It's relief from something they never feel. [pause]

That's why tomorrow isn't a sacrifice. You're not giving anything up. You're putting down something that's been quietly taking from you, many times a day. [pause] Free, not deprived.

Then there's the fear underneath it: I'll be miserable. Here I want to be straight with you. The first few days can be uncomfortable. Cravings come. You might feel snappy, restless, foggy or hungrier than usual. Sleep might be off for a bit. That's withdrawal, and it's real.

But it has an end. For most people it's strongest in the first week, and most of it eases within two to four weeks. [pause] Discomfort that has an end is very different from misery. And every craving you ride out is one fewer ahead of you.

chapters.title: Your break, and your weight
chapters.text:
Next: I'll lose my break.

Here's a question. Is it the nicotine you'd miss, or the five minutes? [pause] Stepping outside. Leaving the desk. A breath of air. A moment that belongs to you.

You keep all of that. The break was never the problem. You can still step out, stand in the sun, take five minutes with a drink or a friend. The only part that's leaving is the part that brought the gap back an hour later. [pause] So tomorrow, take your breaks. Just take them as someone who doesn't need anything from them.

And then, for a lot of people, the quiet one: I'll gain weight.

It's a fair worry, so here are the honest facts. Some weight gain after quitting is common. A large review of studies in the BMJ, looking at people who quit smoking, found the average was about nine to eleven pounds over the first year. But the range was wide. Some people gained very little, and about one in six lost weight. [pause] It isn't a given. Regular meals, water close by and something crunchy for when your hands want something all go a long way. We'll come back to them.

chapters.title: Who am I without it?
chapters.text:
The last fear is the deepest one. Who am I without it?

Maybe it's been part of your day for years. The first thing in the morning. Something to do with your hands. How you pause, how you celebrate, how you get through the hard bits. It can feel like part of who you are. [pause]

But think back. There was a version of you before you ever {s: lit one | v: took a puff | p: put one in}. That person laughed, worked, got bored, got through hard days. Nothing essential about you came from nicotine. [pause]

What you care about is still yours. Think of the reason you chose at the start of the week, the one that matters most. Hold it for a moment now. [long pause] That reason says far more about who you are than a habit ever did.

Tomorrow you don't become someone else. You become someone who doesn't need it.

chapters.title: Today and tonight
chapters.text:
So here's where we are. [pause] The fears are real feelings. But look closely, and most of them are the addiction talking. You'd miss the relief, not a pleasure. Your breaks stay. Weight is manageable. You stay you. [pause]

When one of those thoughts comes back today, and it might, try saying it this way: "I'm having the thought that I'll miss it." Then let it sit there. A thought isn't an order. [pause]

For now, use as normal. Later, you'll clear things out and write a line to tomorrow-you. And this evening I'll be with you for the last one, with your eyes fully open. [pause]

[softly] One more day of seeing clearly. Then you get to stop.

deck.title: What the first week can feel like
deck.intro: Withdrawal is real, and it has an end. Here's what to expect, honestly, and what helps.

cards.front: When does it start, and when is it worst?
cards.answer:
It can start within a few hours of your last {product}. For most people it's strongest in the first days to a week, then it weakens the longer you go without.

A few hours · Withdrawal can start
First week · Withdrawal is usually at its strongest
cards.deeper: Nicotine doesn't last long in the body. Its half-life is about two hours, so the level falls steadily between doses. That falling level is the gap you've watched all week, and it's why the first one of the morning feels so strong. From tomorrow nothing refills it. Within a few hours your brain notices, and that's when the first cravings, restlessness or a short fuse tend to show up. It's uncomfortable, and it's also the sign your body has started adjusting. The first days are the steepest part for most people, which is why your support is front-loaded: Craving SOS, your plans, and a short session every day.

cards.answer: Cravings that come in waves. Irritable or restless. Low or anxious. Harder to focus. Hungrier. Sleep a bit off. Not everyone gets all of these. They're signs of adjusting.
cards.deeper: These are the symptoms that research has confirmed as genuine nicotine withdrawal. Cravings rise, peak and fall, usually within minutes. Irritability is one of the most common, so it's worth warning the people around you. Low mood or anxiety can show up early; for most people, 1 to 2 weeks · Mood changes from withdrawal usually ease. If low mood hangs around longer than that, talk to a doctor. You don't have to push through it alone. Focus can feel foggy for a few days, so take the day in small pieces. Hunger is common: keep easy snacks around. Sleep can be restless at first and usually settles.
cards.source: Hughes, Nicotine Tob Res 2007; smokefree.gov (Managing nicotine withdrawal)

cards.answer:
Most symptoms ease within two to four weeks. Cravings can last a little longer, but they come less often and feel weaker as the weeks go by.

1 to 2 weeks · Mood changes from withdrawal usually ease
A few weeks · Cravings come less often
cards.deeper: Think of it as a slope, not a wall. The first week is the climb. After that, most of the physical side settles, usually within two to four weeks. Cravings are the part that can stay a little longer: “Cravings can last longer than the physical symptoms, but they come less often and feel weaker as the weeks go by.” That's why the program keeps going after Day Xero, with skills for the moments that still turn up. Every wave you ride is practice your brain keeps. Tonight it can feel as if the hard part will last forever. It won't. It has a shape, and you'll be watching it get smaller.
cards.source: Hughes, Nicotine Tob Res 2007; smokefree.gov (Nicotine withdrawal)

cards.answer: Riding each wave instead of fighting it. Food, water and sleep. Moving a little. Telling people. NRT, if you've chosen it. And Craving SOS, one tap away.
cards.deeper: Match the help to the feeling. A craving: notice it, name it, breathe slowly and ride it, or open Craving SOS. Irritable: tell people ahead of time, and try two slow sighs (two breaths in through the nose, one long breath out) before you answer. Foggy: short lists, one task at a time, a walk outside. Hungry: regular meals, water first, crunchy snacks. Sleep: coffee before noon, screens down earlier. {s: And halve your coffee for now: after you stop smoking, the same cup hits harder. | v: Keep an eye on how much coffee you drink if sleep is off. | p: Keep an eye on how much coffee you drink if sleep is off.} If you're using NRT, a patch plus a fast-acting form works better than one alone. Follow the pack.
cards.source: Balban, Cell Rep Med 2023; Cochrane review of combination NRT, 2019{s: ; Benowitz, Hall & Modin, BMJ 1989 | v: | p: }

deck.title: Fears
deck.intro: Five things people fear the night before. Tap Myth or Fact.

statements.text: If I quit, I'll definitely gain a lot of weight.
statements.verdict: Some gain is common. A lot isn't a given.
statements.explanation: It's a fair worry, and the honest answer is in between. A large review found people who quit smoking gained about 4 to 5 kg (9 to 11 lb) on average over the first year, with a wide range: some gained little, and about 16 in 100 lost weight. Hunger is a normal part of withdrawal, so plan for it: regular meals, water close by, something crunchy for your hands. {s: | v: That research looked at people who smoked. There's less on vaping. | p: That research looked at people who smoked. There's less on pouches.}
statements.source: Aubin et al., BMJ 2012; Hughes, Nicotine Tob Res 2007

statements.text: Withdrawal lasts for months.
statements.verdict: For most people, the worst is over in weeks.
statements.explanation: Withdrawal is usually strongest in the first week. Most symptoms, like irritability, restlessness and trouble focusing, ease within two to four weeks. Cravings can hang around a little longer, but they come less often and feel weaker as the weeks go by. So the hard part has an end, and it's nearer than it feels tonight. Each wave you ride brings it closer.
statements.source: Hughes, Nicotine Tob Res 2007; smokefree.gov (health timeline: “A few weeks · Cravings come less often”)

statements.text: I'll never enjoy a coffee or a drink again.
statements.verdict: The link is learned, and it can loosen.
statements.explanation: Coffee and nicotine feel joined because they've happened together thousands of times. The first few coffees without it may feel strange, and that's the old pairing showing itself, not something missing from the coffee. {s: One real change: after you stop smoking, caffeine hits harder, so try half your usual for a while. | v: Give it some time. | p: Give it some time.} In studies of people who quit smoking, mood and quality of life went up on average, not down.
statements.source: Taylor et al., BMJ 2014{s: ; Benowitz, Hall & Modin, BMJ 1989 | v: | p: }

statements.text: I'll always miss it.
statements.verdict: Missing it fades as the gap does.
statements.explanation: What people miss at first is mostly relief: the gap closing. Once nicotine stops arriving, the gap stops being refilled, and cravings come less often and feel weaker as the weeks go by. Wanting it was never proof that it gave you something. It was proof that it took something first. You don't have to feel nothing to be free. You just have to keep letting the waves pass.
statements.source: smokefree.gov (health timeline: “A few weeks · Cravings come less often”); Benowitz, NEJM 2010

deck.title: The last one
deck.intro: About 7 minutes. Have your last one ready, or just listen if you've already had it.

script.voice: Quiet, slow and present, like sitting beside someone in the evening; curious rather than solemn, no drama about "the last one." Around 120 words a minute, leaving the long pauses fully open.

chapters.title: Before you begin
chapters.text:
[calmly] This is the last one. [pause] Not a goodbye. Just one last look, with the lights on.

Get it ready now, and find somewhere you can be for a few minutes. {s: Take one cigarette and your lighter, and go where you'd usually smoke. | v: Have your vape with you, and sit where you'd usually use it. | p: Have one pouch ready, and sit somewhere comfortable.} Leave everything else where it is for now. [long pause]

And if you've already had your last one today, or you'd rather not have one at all, that's completely fine. You don't need one more to be ready. Just listen, and picture it as we go.

Before you start, notice how you feel right now. [pause] Is there a pull? Where is it? Chest, hands, mouth? [pause] A little excitement, maybe, or nerves, or not much at all. Whatever's there, let it be. You're not here to judge anything tonight. Just to see it clearly.

Take one slow breath before you start. In through your nose. [pause] And out. [long pause]

chapters.title: With your eyes open
chapters.text:
{s: Hold the cigarette for a moment before you light it. Look at it. Paper, a filter, dried leaf. | v: Hold the vape for a moment. Look at it. A battery, a coil, a little liquid. | p: Hold the pouch for a moment. Look at it. A small white packet with some filler and flavoring.} [pause] This small thing has had first call on your attention, many times a day, for a long time.

Now {s: light it, and take the first drag slowly. | v: take the first puff, slowly. | p: put it in, the way you usually do.} [pause]

What do you notice first? [pause] {s: The heat. The taste. The smoke in your throat and chest. | v: The vapor. The sweetness. The catch at the back of your throat. | p: The tingle. Maybe a burn on your gum. The taste.} [long pause]

Now notice the relief. That small settling, a few seconds later. [pause] That's the gap closing. The restlessness the last one left behind, being topped up. [pause] The relief is real. And it's the whole trick. It soothes a feeling it created.

{s: Keep going at your own pace. With each drag, notice the heat and the taste. | v: Take a few more puffs, at your own pace. Notice each one. | p: Let it sit. Every so often, notice the taste and the tingle, and whether they're changing.} [long pause]

Ask yourself, honestly: is it as good as the story says? [pause] Better? Worse? About the same as all the others? There's no right answer. Only your answer. [long pause]

And notice your mind, too. Is it already somewhere else? Planning, scrolling, thinking about tomorrow? [pause] That's how most of them have gone. Half-noticed, on autopilot. Tonight, this one gets your full attention. [long pause]

chapters.title: What's left
chapters.text:
{s: When you're done, put it out properly. | v: When you've had your last puff, put the vape down. | p: Take the pouch out whenever you're done, and put it in the bin. You can keep listening while it sits.} [pause] Take a slow breath. [long pause]

Now notice what's left. [pause] {s: The taste in your mouth. The smell on your fingers. | v: The sweetness fading. Maybe a dry mouth. | p: The taste fading. The tingle wearing off.} [pause] And notice how quickly the good part went. A few seconds of relief, and then back to ordinary. [pause] Give it an hour or so, and the gap would start to open again. Then another one to close it. That's the loop you've been in, many times a day, for years. Not because you're weak. Because that's how nicotine works.

Right now, all over the world, people who don't use nicotine are having an ordinary evening without any of this. They're not missing it. [pause] They don't have a gap to close.

From tomorrow, nothing refills yours. There'll be waves, especially at first. But each one you ride shows your body and your brain that they can do without. [pause]

That was the last one.

chapters.title: Clearing the way
chapters.text:
Now the rest goes. {s: Any cigarettes left, run them under the tap and put them in the bin. Lighters and ashtrays too. | v: Your vape, the pods and the charger go together, set aside for battery recycling. Please don't put them in the bin. | p: Any tins left go in the bin. Check your bag, your car and your desk.} If you ticked these off earlier, check one more time. [long pause]

Notice what shows up as you do it. A flicker of panic? A voice saying "keep one, just in case"? [pause] That's the addiction having its say. You can hear it, and still not do what it says. A thought isn't an order. [pause] You've practiced this all week. Notice it, name it, let it be there, and keep going.

And notice the other feeling too, if it's there. A little lighter. A little more room. [pause] That's what's coming.

chapters.title: Ready
chapters.text:
[softly] Some nerves tonight are normal. They don't mean anything is wrong. Go easy on yourself. Have some water. Get to bed at a sensible time. If a craving shows up before you sleep, Craving SOS is there, and the wave will pass.

Tomorrow morning, read your note first. Then I'll walk you into the day. Your plan for the first hour is already made. And if you're using a patch, put it somewhere you'll see it when you wake.

You've spent seven days looking at this with your eyes open. You've seen the gap, the autopilot, the stories, and the wave. That was the hard part. Tomorrow is mostly just not refilling it.

When you're ready, press and hold the button on your screen for three seconds. [pause] That's you saying it. Not "I'll try." Just: I'm ready. [long pause]

script.voice: Warm, grounded and quietly confident, a calm morning voice with a little lift in it; no hype, no solemnity. About 130 words a minute, slowing for the breaths at the end.

chapters.title: Good morning
chapters.text:
[warmly] Good morning. If you wrote a note last night, you've just read it. [pause] Take a second with it. That was you, looking out for you.

Today is Day Xero. [pause] And before anything else, I'd like you to hear this. The hardest part is already behind you. For seven days you've looked at nicotine with your eyes open. You've seen the gap, the autopilot, the stories. You've seen that the relief was mostly the gap closing, and that the gap was made by the last dose. [pause]

So today you're not losing anything. You're simply not refilling it. You're not someone who can't {s: smoke | v: vape | p: use pouches} today. You're someone who doesn't need to. [pause]

Maybe you woke up feeling calm, even a little excited. Maybe you woke up nervous, already bracing for the first craving. Both are completely normal. How you feel this morning doesn't decide how today goes. [pause]

chapters.title: What today might hold
chapters.text:
Let's be honest about today, so nothing catches you off guard.

At some point in the next few hours, your body will notice the nicotine isn't coming. That's usually when the first cravings show up. You might feel restless, a bit irritable, or find it harder to focus. You might be hungrier than usual. [pause] Those are normal signs of your body adjusting. They're usually strongest in the first days, and they ease. None of it means something's going wrong. It means something has started. [pause]

Here's a way to see it. The gap you've watched all week is going to open today, and this time nothing will fill it. That's most of the discomfort: the same gap you already know, just left open. And the longer it's left open, the more your body gets used to living without it. [pause]

And quietly, in the background, other things are starting too. {s: Within minutes of stopping, your heart rate and blood pressure start to come down. And over the next few days, the carbon monoxide in your blood drops back to normal. | v: Nicotine itself clears from your blood within hours, and within a few days most of what's left is gone. | p: Nicotine itself clears from your blood within hours, and within a few days most of what's left is gone.} You'll see more of that in the next step.

So take today in small pieces. Not forever. Just this morning. Then lunch. Then the afternoon.

chapters.title: Your first craving
chapters.text:
Now, the first craving. Let's plan for it, so it doesn't surprise you. [pause]

It might come with your first coffee, after breakfast, in the car, or the first time you sit down to work. Last night you made a plan for the first one. When it comes, use it.

And then, this. Notice it. [pause] Name it: "There's a craving." [pause] Find where it sits in your body. Chest, hands, mouth, stomach. [pause] Let it be there. You don't have to fight it, and you don't have to do what it says. [pause] Breathe slowly, a little longer out than in. And watch it like a wave. It rises, it peaks, and it falls, usually within a few minutes. [pause]

If you'd like company while it passes, open Craving SOS. It's always in the bar at the bottom of the app, and you'll try a practice run in a few minutes, so you know exactly what to expect. When the wave has passed, tap "It passed." [pause] Every one you ride teaches your brain that it can.

chapters.title: If it gets hard
chapters.text:
Some moments today might be tough. That's not a sign you're doing it wrong. It's what a first day can feel like. [pause] So, a few things to keep close.

If you're using nicotine replacement, use it the way your pack says. It takes the edge off the physical side, and it isn't cheating. Not using it is fine too.

Tell someone that today's the day. A message back from a friend can carry you through a wave.

Eat proper meals, keep water close, and if you drink coffee, {s: have about half your usual. Now that you've stopped smoking, the same cup hits harder. | v: notice whether it leaves you jittery. That can feel a lot like a craving. | p: notice whether it leaves you jittery. That can feel a lot like a craving.}

And if you slip, [pause] it doesn't wipe anything out. Your count isn't reset. Tap "I slipped," be kind to yourself, notice what set it off, and carry on from right there. A slip is information, not the end of anything. The very next choice is the one that matters.

chapters.title: Starting
chapters.text:
[calmly] So, here you are. [pause] Take a slow breath in. [pause] And a long breath out. [long pause]

Think of your reason. The one that matters most. [long pause]

Now picture today going the way you'd like it to. Not perfectly. Just one wave at a time, each one passing. [long pause]

When you're ready, press and hold the button on your screen for three seconds. When you let go, your counter starts, and Day Xero begins. [pause]

You're not losing anything today. You're getting through one day, one wave at a time. [pause] I'll be with you this evening.

cards.front: What starts the moment you stop?

answer.smoking: Within minutes · Heart rate and blood pressure start to come down. From your first smoke-free hours. You may not feel it, but it has already begun.
answer.vaping: A few hours · Withdrawal can start. Cravings, restlessness or irritability are common. Uncomfortable, yes. It's also the first sign your body is adjusting.

deeper.smoking: Nicotine keeps your heart working a little harder all day: a little faster, with a little more pressure in every beat. The timeline puts it simply: “Soon after your last cigarette, your heart rate and blood pressure begin to settle.” You won't feel fireworks. Some people notice a calmer chest or warmer hands; plenty notice nothing at all, and it's happening either way. Slow breathing goes well with it, which is one reason the next step is a breathing practice. More changes follow over the coming weeks, and you can watch them arrive in Progress.

It feels uncomfortable, but it's a good sign: your body has started adjusting to life without nicotine. Each wave rises, peaks and passes, usually within a few minutes. You don't have to make it stop. You only have to let it pass without doing what it says, and Craving SOS is there to ride it with you. You'll practice that in the next step.

cards.deeper: Not everyone gets all of these, and they come and go. Here's what helps today. Cravings: notice, name, breathe, ride, or open Craving SOS. Restless: move. A walk around the block counts. Snappy: tell the people around you it's Day Xero, and take two slow sighs before you answer. Foggy: one task at a time, a short list, and no big decisions you can put off. Hungry: proper meals and easy snacks, like fruit, nuts or crunchy veg. And keep water close: a glass gives your hands and mouth something to do while a wave passes.

cards.front: How long will it feel like this?
cards.answer: First week · Withdrawal is usually at its strongest. The hardest stretch for most people. After that it weakens, and most symptoms ease within two to four weeks.
cards.deeper: Today is the first day of the steepest part, so it's normal if it feels like a lot. It won't stay like this. The timeline puts it this way: “For most people, withdrawal is strongest in the first days to week, then weakens the longer you stay nicotine-free.” Most symptoms ease within two to four weeks. Cravings can last a little longer, but they come less often and feel weaker as the weeks go by. That's why every day of Week 1 has a short session, built for exactly where you are.

chapters.title: You're here
chapters.text:
[warmly] It's the evening of Day Xero. [pause] However today went, you're here, and you're listening. That counts for a lot.

Maybe it was easier than you expected. Maybe parts of it were hard. Maybe there was a moment when you slipped. [pause] All of those are real first days. If you did slip, nothing has been reset. Your days still count, and tomorrow still begins from here. [pause]

Wherever you are, get comfortable. If you're already in bed, that's perfect. Let your shoulders drop. [pause] Unclench your jaw. [pause]

Let's take a few minutes together. We'll look back, look after tonight, and look ahead.

chapters.title: What today was
chapters.text:
Think back over the day. [pause] When did the first craving come? [pause] What set it off? Coffee, a meal, the phone, a stressful moment? [pause] And what did you do? [long pause]

Every time a craving rose today and you didn't follow it, your brain learned something new. This passes. I'm okay. [pause] That's not a small thing. It's how the next one gets a little quieter.

And notice what helped. Was it the breathing? Water? A walk? Texting someone? Just keeping busy? [pause] Whatever worked today is worth keeping. Tomorrow, reach for it first.

And you might have noticed something else. Between the waves, there were stretches where you weren't thinking about it at all. Maybe only a few minutes at a time. [pause] That's what free feels like at first. Small pieces. They get bigger.

If today felt like one long craving, that happens too, especially on a first day. It doesn't mean it'll always feel like this. The first week is the steepest part, and you've just done the first day of it.

And think about the gap. Today, nothing refilled it. That's part of why it was loud at times. It's also why, from here, it starts to fade.

Before we move on, think of one moment today you're quietly proud of. It doesn't have to be big. [long pause] Hold on to that one.

chapters.title: Tonight
chapters.text:
Now, tonight. [pause]

Sleep can be a bit different for a while. Some people find it harder to drop off, or wake more in the night, in the first days. It's common, and it usually settles. A few things help. Keep coffee to the morning. {s: It hits harder now that you've stopped smoking. | v: Late caffeine and a restless night don't mix. | p: Late caffeine and a restless night don't mix.} Dim the screens a little earlier. And if you're lying awake, slow your breathing: in for four, out for six.

Evenings can feel a bit strange at first. If you'd usually wind down with {s: a cigarette | v: the vape | p: a pouch}, the evening might feel oddly empty. That's the gap again, and the autopilot looking for its old cue. Give the evening something new to hold instead. A shower. Something warm to drink, without caffeine. A few pages of a book. A walk around the block.

If you're using a patch, your pack will say whether it stays on overnight or comes off at bedtime. If you get vivid dreams or broken sleep, taking it off at bedtime often helps, as long as your pack says you can.

If you used to {s: smoke | v: vape | p: have a pouch} before bed, expect that cue to show up tonight. If a craving comes, it's the same as today. Notice it, name it, breathe, and let it pass. Craving SOS works in the dark too.

chapters.title: Tomorrow
chapters.text:
Tomorrow, Week 1 begins. [pause] The first few days are usually the toughest stretch, so tomorrow is about looking after the basics. Food. Water. Sleep. [pause] Being hungry, thirsty or tired can feel a lot like a craving. When those are looked after, the real cravings are easier to spot, and easier to ride.

So tonight, one small thing. Put a glass of water by your bed. And think about what you'll have for breakfast. [long pause]

Last night, your note was waiting for you this morning. Tomorrow you'll wake up with something better than a note. You'll have a whole day behind you.

Over the coming weeks, the waves will keep coming for a while, but less often, and with less force. Some days will be easier than others, and a hard day doesn't undo the good ones. Each morning there'll be a short session waiting for you, built for exactly where you are.

chapters.title: One day
chapters.text:
[softly] Before you go, let's breathe together, just three times. [pause] In through your nose. [pause] And slowly out. [long pause] Again. In. [pause] And out. [long pause] One more. In. [pause] And all the way out. [long pause]

One day. Last night it was something you were getting ready for. Tonight it's something you've done. [pause] You didn't need to be perfect. You needed to keep coming back to the next choice. And you're still here, coming back.

And if a thought shows up tonight, something like "just one wouldn't hurt," you know what it is now. A thought, not an order. You can let it sit there and go to sleep anyway. [pause]

Thank yourself for today. Really. [pause] Sleep well. I'll see you tomorrow.
